In his last letter THE BULLETIN's regular Washington correspondent says: "Our present and prospective relations with Mexico are being made a study by the secretary of state. He sees the probability that difficulties will arise from the vast amount of our capital now being invested in that country, and from the emigration which is just beginning but which promises to become great. While this government is not in any way connected with these movements, and congress wisely ignored the request of Captain Eads to guarantee the bonds for his marine railway across Mexican territory, the secretary knows that we may at any moment be called upon to protect our citizens in Mexico. The turn of affairs is so sudden and unprecedented that the administration in the event of trouble, will have to work out an entirely new course of action." He says further: "Secretary Blaine and Sir Edward Thornton, the British minister, have concluded negotiations by which the British government is bound to pay £15,000 sterling to the United States, to indemnify American fishermen who suffered loss by the Fortune bay outrage."

About eleven o'clock night before last the young negro, who committed the outrage upon Mrs. Kobler, was captured at his home, at the corner of Twenty-ninth and Sycamore streets. Sheriff Hodges, Marshal Myers and Officer John Tyler were engaged in the hunt and it was greatly due to the latter that the fellow was discovered and captured as soon as he was found. The officers had but very little clue to work upon and therefore deserve much credit for making the capture with such dispatch. The young wretche's name is Albert Hayes; he is quite black, weighed about a hundred and fifty pounds and is about nineteen years of age. He has served a term in the state reform school, from which he was discharged about last Christmas. Yesterday in the presence of Sheriff Hodges and Marshal Myers he made a full confession of his crime, which coincides almost entirely with the account published in yesterday's BULLETIN; with the exception that he denies having dragged his victim to the pond by the hair of her head. The wounds about her head, he said, were caused by her fall. His preliminary trial will probably come off to-morrow.

ATTEMPT AT LYNCHING.
Although during the past few days numerous threats have been heard which did not bode well for the young negro, Albert Hayes, who recently assaulted Mrs. Kobler a short distance above the city, it was generally believed that no effort would be made which would tend to curtail the young rascal's earthly existence. About one o'clock yesterday morning, however, a body of masked men—numbering about forty—gathered at the county jail with the fixed determination of mobbing the negro.

The mob approached the jail very quietly and found no difficulty in gaining an entrance, since the outside doors had been left open on account of the excessive heat. Having reached the hall, where Mike and John Fitzgerald, sons of our coroner, were asleep, they cov-
albert-hayes-1881-06-07.A4: ered the young men with their weapons before they had an opportunity of rising, and demanded the keys of the jail, whereupon Mike, arising from the cot, ran into the kitchen for the apparent purpose of procuring the keys but really for the purpose of giving the alarm. He was however, closely followed and his object becoming apparent, he was surrounded and threatened with instant death unless he procured the keys. At this juncture his brother, John who had also been permitted to leave his bed, put in an appearance with a shotgun and leveling it at the crowd, demanded his brother's release, which demand was complied with. John then escaped from the building and making his way across the street secured the assistance of his father, Mr. Richard Fitzgerald, who, having already heard the noise created by the mob, shortly afterwards put in an appearance. Before his arrival however, the mob had been actively at work making their way to the young criminal. They had already, with a crow-bar and axe, broken open the door by which the hall way leading to the negro's cell is reached and had also destroyed two of the three locks to the cell door which parted them from the object of their search, when Mr. Fitzgerald put in an appearance and demanded that they vacate the building—very emphatically, telling them at the same time that they could not obtain the prisoner without inflicting bodily injury upon him. Mr. Fitzgerald was unarmed, but was perfectly cool and fully determined that the prisoner should not be taken, and by his conduct convinced the mob that they must inflict injury upon him and his sons before their object could be obtained. Upon entering the jail Mr. Fitzgerald had ordered that the fire bells be rung tor assistance, and the clanging of the bells, which now commenced, also probably, had some effect upon the crowd which had already shown signs of weakening. At any rate the mob speedily dispursed and the axe and crow bar was heaved over the court yard fence after them.

It was rumored late last night that another attempt to do personal violence to the negro, Albert Hayes, would be made early this morning. That twelve men from Kentucky had been imported to do the job of hanging the young wretch. Up to this writing, half-past eleven o'clock, all is quiet and no attempt has been made to repeat the rather grotesque affair of the night before. That there is ample cause for indignation at the heinous crime of the youthful devil cannot be doubted, but it is also a crime to take him out of the hands of the law after he has been placed under lock and key with the intention of sending him prematurely into hades.

Albert Hayes, the young negro, whose blood was sought by a company of angry citizens night before last, was taken to the county court room for a preliminary examination yesterday afternoon. Esquire Osborn was present and held court. The negro was represented by Hon. D. T. Linegar and the people by City Attorney Hendricks. The prisoner waived an examination, and was held in bond in the sum of five hundred dollars for his appearance at the July term of the circuit court. He was very much scared at the attempt made upon his life the night before, and therefore he was not brought to the police court for trial.

A woman named Goulding was burned to death a day or two by the explosion of coal oil, which was sold for 130 fire test, but which proved to be only 105 when tested. The law of Kentucky does not permit the sale of any burning fluid for family use that will explode at less than one hundred and thirty degrees Fahrenheit. In Illinois this does not appear to be the case, as great quantities of coal oil of no more than one hundred and ten degrees fire test, are being daily sold in this city as well as elsewhere.

CINCINNATI'S MAYOR.

Ha Has Become Very Unpopular with the Democrats—They Propose to Hold a Public Meeting and Denounce His Conduct Since His Elevation to Office.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

CINCINNATI, O., May 23.—A hall has been hired and a meeting called by a number of Democrats of this city for the purpose of denouncing the policy of the Reform Mayor, Mr. William Means. The meeting will be held on Saturday night next, and is called by some of the most prominent Democrats who are accustomed to mix in local politics. The complaint against Mayor Means is, that he is untrue to the party who elected him, and it is proposed to formally announce his disloyalty at a public meeting called for that purpose, and to give him back to the easy-going and wealthy clique from whom he came. The Mayor was elected six weeks ago by a combination of the Democratic party and a considerable class of Republicans who were anxious to see certain reforms carried out touching liquor-selling and the observance of the Sabbath. Means, it was thought by the Democrats, could be easily handled, and half a dozen of the old party leaders each flattered himself that he would be the new Mayor's confidential adviser and the power behind the throne. When elected, however, Mr. Means announced that he wanted no advice from anybody, and, though supported by the whole Democratic party, would give none of its leaders a hearing as to how the patronage should be distributed. A few Democratic politemen received appointments, but it was entirely through their own efforts. Those who depended upon the leaders of the party for recommendation and assistance had no attention paid to their applications. "The same was true of applicants for other offices, and the rank and file of the party, as well as its leaders, have naturally became very sore, and the step which they have now resolved to take has been talked of for some time. The Reform Republicans have been better satisfied with the Mayor's course, for the reason that there has been some effort at reform, although the results are hardly appreciable. The Mayor is a life-long Democrat, but knows nothing about politics, and, being of an obstinate disposition, he got his party by the ears at the very outset. The effect, of course, has been to greatly strengthen the Republicans. The Democratic victory at the spring election, unexpectedly to everybody, is proving to be one of the best things for the Republican party that could have happened.

Some time ago there arrived in this city a young man who gave his name as Walch de Serrant. He said he was a count, all the way from France, and as his manners were very smooth and ingratiating, his story obtained wide credence. He fell into bad ways, however, and in consequence became intimately acquainted with the criminal laws of Texas, Arkansas and Louisiana. The editor of the Little Rock Gazette "wrote up" the court in a very laughable manner, and the victim swore that he would be avenged upon the writer as soon as he had righted himself in the eyes of the public. His counsel took an appeal to the Supreme Court, and yesterday the verdict and judgment of the lower court was affirmed. Justice Todd, who read the decision of the Supreme Court, took occasion to say in the course of his remarks:

We have closely scrutinized the proceedings pertaining to this prosecution, and we cannot find a single right or privilege guaranteed to an accused by law that was denied the defendant, but on the contrary that every means of defense in the power of the court was afforded him, and we find no error or irregularity in any part of the proceeding.

The count will take a visit up the river as far as Baton Rouge, where in the privacy and reclusion of the penitentiary or work on the road he will have ample time and opportunity to perfect his bellicose arrangements for the annihilation of the Arkansas editor who gave him such a beautiful send off in his paper.

AN ALABAMA RIOT.

Two Negroes Killed by Officers of the Law.

Jacksonville (Ill.) Republican.

Last Saturday, as usual on that day in Anniston, several hundred negroes and white men gathered there. It seems there was more than the usual amount of drinking done that day by the negroes, and early in the morning quite a body of them evinced a riotous disposition.

About 12 o'clock the Marshal had occasion to arrest a negro whom no had been ordered to bring before H. L. Jeffers, Esq., for carrying concealed weapons. When the arrest was made, the negroes assumed such a threatening attitude that the Marshal was compelled to strike one with a club to keep the crowd off him. After trial this man was incarcerated in the calaboose until arrangements could be made for sending him to jail. Subsequently the Marshal arrested another negro, and started with him to the calaboose. He was followed again and closely pressed by a howling, profane gang of negroes who were urging the prisoner not to suffer himself to be incarcerated.

They pressed around and about the Marshal and his deputy from the place of arrest to the calaboose, and by the time of his arrival there they pressed him so closely he did not have time to unlock the prison door. At this juncture a white man named Mulke pressed forward and took the keys. The Marshal faced the crowd, and, drawing his pistol, ordered them to stand back or he would fire.

At this juncture Greenwood, the leader of the rioters, sprang forward and struck the Marshal with a rock, making a rather severe wound on the head and nearly bringing him to the ground. The Marshal fired upon him at once and shot him down. At the same instant the Deputy Marshal (Smith) opened fire on the rioters, and the prisoner (Hammond) who was making his way to where the Marshal and Greenwood were engaged, was shot, and, running up a flight of several steps, fell. There were four shots fired and two negroes shot, one of whom died instantly and the other the following Monday morning.

The Justice of the Peace, Mr. Jeffers, held an inquest over the body of Hammond and subsequently that of Greenwood, the verdict of the jury being in the latter case that he came to his death at the hands of officers of the law while in the lawful discharge of their duty.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES
Thomas Garfield, an Uncle of the President, Killed by the Cars--A Party of Lynchers in Michigan Foiled by the Sheriff's Wife--Great Destruction of Grain, Farm Houses and Machinery by Fire in California--The Daily Record.

FOILED BY A PLUCKY WOMAN.

DETROIT, June 22.—A second attempt was made at an early hour this morning to reach and lynch Waskamp, lying in jail at Grand Haven, who shot his employer, Lyman Cady, about a month ago at Lamont. Some dozen of the most respected farmers of that vicinity suddenly appeared at the jail at the hour named, overpowered the deputy sheriff and compelled him to give them the keys to the murderer's cell. They then all went in and secured their victim. The sheriff's wife, aroused by the noise, in the absence of her husband from town, went to the spot, discovered the situation, closed the outside door of the jail, which the lynching party had left unguarded, and bagged the whole lot. She then sent a servant girl to ring the fire alarm, which called out the citizens and completely frustrated the attempt.

SHOOTING AFFRAY.

COUNCIL BLUFFS, June 22.—Between three and four this afternoon a fatal shooting affray occurred in the office of the Ogden hotel, in which Harry McGee, head waiter at the Pacific hotel, shot and instantly killed Geo. Washington, waiter at the Ogden house. Both were colored. McGee followed Washington into the hotel after having a scuffle with him outside, and, drawing a revolver, deliberately fired, the ball taking effect in or close to his heart, from which Washington died in a moment or two. McGee was arrested. The trouble originated over a colored woman with whom both were in love. Yesterday McGee hunted for Washington and threatened then to kill him.
STRUCK BY AN ENGINE.
BROCTON, Mass., June 22.—As the 8 o'clock train from Fall River approached Huntington Heights station a hack driven by Mr. Early was struck by the engine, demolishing it. Early was thrown twenty-five feet and killed, and the two occupants of the carriage, James Bennett and J. Shields, were terribly injured, probably fatally. Both horses were killed.

DROWNED.
CHICAGO, June 22.—Samuel Randall, a hostler, and Hall, a colored man, drove into the river this forenoon to wash a buggy, when by some means the horses and men were drowned and the buggy was carried down the stream.

THROUGH A BRIDGE.
FREEPORT, Pa., June 22.—A serious accident occurred here between 4 and 5 o'clock this afternoon. The west bound freight train on the Pennsylvania road ran over a cow near the Buffalo creek bridge, throwing the engine off the track on the bridge, causing the bridge to fall, and precipitating the engine and ten cars into the creek. The engineer, Jas. E. Repine, and the fireman, Jas. Delrich, were both killed. Major Snowden, of Freeport, a passenger, was also killed. The bodies have since been recovered. That of the engineer, was found wedged in the timbers. A brakeman named Gallagher made a narrow escape by jumping off a box car. Repine and Delrich lived at Blaisville, Pa.

BRUTAL DEED.
LITTLE Rock, June 22.—A Gazette specia says a brutal crime occured near Luckanwork day before yesterday, when H. Parnell, aged 60 years of age, raped a little daughter, aged 7, of Maurice Crabb. Parnell had been in the employ of Mr. Crabb as a farm hand some time, and had been received in the father's family. The little girl had been in the habit of carrying out fresh water to the field where the men were at work. Mr. Crabb had occasion to go to the house a short time. Mr. Crabb returned again, and was surprised to find the old man in the act of accomplishing his dreadful purpose. Parnell, on seeing he was detected, ran away, and Mr. Crabb, after caring for the child, gave the alarm to his neighbors. Great indignation prevails, and a large number of citizens went in pursuit. The old man was finally captured in the evening, about four miles from the scene, in a thick wood. Yesterday morning, on being taken before the justice of Jackson, he pleaded guilty to the charge of rape, and was remanded to jail.

GRAIN FIRE.

SAN FRANCISCO, June 22.—A dispatch from Merced, says to-day fires swept over some 7,250 acres of wheat and other grain, destroying everything in its course, including many farm houses and much farming machinery. Loss not known.

AN UNCLE OF THE PRESIDENT KILLED.

CLEVELAND, O., June 22.—Shortly after 3 o'clock this afternoon, the east bound train on the New York, Pennsylvania & Ohio railway, when about twelve miles from here, struck a buggy, in which were riding Thos. Garfield, uncle of President Garfield, and Mrs. Alonzo Arnold, sister of Dr. Boyton, cousin of the President. Thomas Garfield was instantly killed, and Mrs. Arnold's skull so badly fractured life is despaired of. The buggy was dragged about 200 feet before the train stopped. Mr. Garfield was eighty years old. He leaves several children. Gen. Garfield and Dr. Boyton were telegraphed to at Long Branch.

POISONED.

ATLANTA, Ga., June 22.—At a picnic at Decatur thirty-five people were poisoned by eating chicken salad. The chicken had been boiled in a brass kettle. All suffered severely, but no serious consequences resulted.

The homicide was committed near Lake Charles, last spring, and Josephus, after lying out a few days, went to Rapides parish, where he was arrested by the Sheriff of Rapides and lodged in jail at Alexandria. Our sheriff, being informed of the arrest, sent Deputy Sheriff John S. Hawkins to Alexandria, and he soon returned and lodged Josephus in jail at this place. He was tried by jury and convicted by an unqualified verdict. Just before noon on last Friday, by order of District Judge Hon. S. D. Read, he was brought into court to receive sentence of death, his handcuffs and shackles having been removed.

As he sat down in a chair everybody could see by the trembling of the limbs that he was violently agitated, but by a supreme effort he controlled his features so that they presented no evidence of emotion beyond an occasional anxious glance at the open windows near by. He was attended by four deputy sheriffs, one of whom—Richard Coward—carried a Winchester rifle, the others having pistols in their hip pockets.

Sentenced, in due form of law, to be hung by the neck until he was dead, a deputy sheriff took hold of the prisoner's left arm and started to lead him out of the court room, the other deputies following just behind him. As he sprung across the ditch by the road side Coward and another deputy fired almost simultaneously, and Josephus fell. Instantly rising, however, he resumed his race for life, running up the street and past the jail amid a perfect storm of bullets, several of which perforated his shirt within an inch of his body. As he reached Ryan street he turned to the right and ran down that street. As Mr. Coward reached the same corner, and Josephus had nearly reached the next square, a ball from Mr. Coward's rifle struck the fugitive a little back of and over the left ear, glanced around the skull and came out at the face. Frank and John McDonald, two ex-convicts who have just completed an eighteen-months' term in the State prison, and have been out only two weeks, while at a disreputable house in the outskirts of this village, day before yesterday, got into a row with Willie Kittson, a half-breed, about 23 years old. Norman Kittson and one Tommy Dunn went to the relief of Willie, and took him from the house and started for home. The McDonalds followed them and attacked them again on the street. Willie was knocked down and then stabbed several times. Norman received several severe knife wounds in the face and side. Great excitement prevailed from the time of the murder, and extra guards were placed over the jail. The prisoners were pulled out of the cell and long ropes fastened about their necks, and they were then dragged by the mob mercilessly through the street for three-quarters of a mile to the house where the row originated, where their bodies were suspended to a tree. The victims were dead, however, long before their bodies were hung up. The house above mentioned was then set on fire and burned to the ground. The two bodies were left suspended to the tree until this morning, when they were taken down by the authorities. A Man Hunt.
Four counties in southeast Missouri have been deeply agitated over a man hunt. The recent slaughter of a deputy sheriff at Sikeston caused the citizens to undertake the extirpation of four desperadoes named Frank Brown, Jesse Myers, James Hamilton and Patrick Rhoades. The latter was found at a farm-house, badly wounded, and sent back under guard, but never reached Sikeston. In a fight with the others near Greenville, Sheriff Davis and J. F. Hatton were badly wounded, and one thousand armed men turned out. Near Piedmont, Hamilton was killed and Myers captured. Brown subsequently surrendered himself. The captured men were afterward hung by a mob.

Ed. Courier:—I have contemplated writing you for some time, but have neglected to do so. The Courier is ever a welcome visitor, and it is with regret that we learn of your contemplated retirement from its control.

The Bend is quiet. There is not a more peaceable neighborhood in the State. Each one is pursuing the even tenor of his way. Farmers are busy, trying to regain the time lost during the last wet spell of weather. Corn looks well, tho' it is a little later than usual. There is a general complaint of a "bad stand," caused, it is supposed, by the germ being killed by the cold weather of last winter.

Col. R. C. Everett, who is, perhaps, the largest practical farmer in the bend, has 600 acres of corn which looks beautiful. It has been plowed once, and a portion of it, twice.

The prospect for wheat is very flattering. Several heads that I have examined have three and four grains to the mesh. The army worm has made its appearance in some of the wheat-fields, but not in sufficient numbers to cause any alarm.

Our New Madrid neighbors have been greatly excited over the discovery, pursuit and capture of a band of outlaws in that vicinity. The last two of the gang were captured in Wayne county, Mo., last Friday, by Capt. Lesser and an assistant. Before they were captured, they killed a man and little girl near New Madrid, and the sheriff and deputy of Wayne county. They were brought to Madrid last Sunday evening and put in jail. Shortly after dark, while Judge Lynch was organizing his court to hang them in haste and try them at leisure, the sheriff with two or three assistants took them out of jail, carried them around the town to the river, placed them in a skiff and rowed down the river about 3 miles, hailed in the Colorado, got on board and carried them to St. Louis. I hear that much indignation is expressed in consequence of the sheriff's action.

Last week, we had the pleasure of listening to an interesting lecture from Judge Kingman, on the subject of education. Think it will be productive of much good, as he succeeded in arousing the dormant interest of the people on that important subject. Respectfully, M. A. McDANIEL.

The devilish ferocity which southeast Missouri begets in her desperadoes is not more remarkable than the grim expedition with which she meets out retribution for their misdeeds. It is only two months since the New Madrid outlaws committed their first murder. To-day the gang is extinct, as Jesse Myers and Frank Brown, who have just expiated their crimes on the scaffold, were the last survivors of as precious a band of scoundrels as ever defied the law.

The story of their exploits is of blood-cusdling interest. About last Christmas Meyers, Brown, James O. Hamilton and Pat Rhodes were all living in a house near Bain's store, some nine miles from New Madrid. They had evidently at this early day banded together for mischief. Thefts occurred now and then in the vicinity and it was not long before the people began to hint that the quartette were responsible. However, there was no direct proof, and the depredations continued unchecked. Among those who were more outspoken than others, was Wm. Knox, a farmer living five miles south of New Madrid. The gang had several times threatened him but as he didn't scare they determined to make away with him. On the night of the 8th of May, they stealthily approached Knox's house. It was about 8 o'clock, dusk having fallen, but the family being still astir. Keeping well in the shadows of the shrubbery the miscreants were able to approach the house without being discovered. Then skulking under the bushes like wild beasts they watched their opportunity. There was a light in the house. Presently a man with an infant in his arms passed the window. The fatal signal was given, a volley was fired the man fell and the assassins thought their work was done.

They slunk away silently and escaped without being seen but the neighborhood had no doubt as to their identity. It so happened too that the man they had fired on was not Knox, but a visitor named Coleman. Coleman was probably saved from death by the fact that three out of the four bullets discharged struck the infant, while he himself received the fourth in the thigh. The child died in a few days.

Meyers, Brown and Hamilton made their way over into Wayne county. All three were skilled in woodcraft and the country is full of flat, tangled forests in which they had little difficulty in finding safety. The people in all the country around, however, were on the qui vive, and it was not written that they should escape. On the 19th of May, at evening, a travel worn stranger dropped in at Bennet's store in Greenville, the county seat of Wayne county. He was in such a tattered condition that he was taken for a tramp. His shoes were worn out and he bought a new pair which he put on. He then bought another pair, stating that his partner had gone to wake up the ferry man.

This aroused suspicion, and as soon as the man was gone the store-keeper informed Sheriff John T. Davis. Next morning Sheriff Davis and ex-Sheriff James F. Hatton started out to look for the men. They had no difficulty in tracing them to the house of a man named Lee, about a mile from town. Dismounting from their horses they quietly approached the house, being pretty well satisfied by this time that these were two of the New Madrid outlaws. The officers were well armed, but as they stepped in at the door the two men were eating breakfast and apparently at their mercy. So it did not seem that any display of weapons was necessary. Without ceremony they commanded the two to rise. The command was obeyed, but both men, who were Meyers and Hamilton, came up with a navy revolver in each hand and began to shoot without saving a word. Davis fell instantly with a bullet in his head and Hatton received a glancing wound on his skull which crazed him for the time being. He succeeded in mounting his horse and reaching town where his incoherent story created the wildest excitement. Another $2,000 reward was offered and 500 men turned out to scour the country for them. The same night, Brown, the third man, was cornered by a posse but managed to slip through their fingers somehow. Davis was at first reported dead but eventually both he and Hatton recovered.

As the news of this astounding succession of crimes spread the people of three counties wiped out their shotguns and squirrel rifles and trod the field in squads. Col. W. T. Leeper, of Mill Springs, had charge of one of the parties, his comrades being Ambrose Beatty, Cal Thomas and Taylor Fulton. Col. Leeper made up his mind that the desperadoes would try to cross Black river under cover of darkness at which is known as Campbell's switch. He accordingly posted his men and ambushed the crossings. The watchers had a weary vigil of it all night, but just as dawn was breaking two men came walking up the railroad towards the river. As the pair came along they thought at first that they were citizens scouting, but when they were quite near and were seen to be strangers of a very trampish cut the loud command was gived, "hold on there!" At the word Meyers and Hamilton, for it proved to be they, wheeled and threw up their shotguns ready to kill on the instant. But this time somebody else had the drop, and they had met some one as quick on the trigger as themselves. At the first move they made with their weapons there was a regular fusillade, and both men were cut down like weeds before a sickle. Hamilton stopped ten backshot, and Meyers was badly wounded in the head. Hamilton never moved. The ugly life was driven out of him by the leaden bullets. Neither of the bandits had fired, but both dropped with their double-barreled shotguns cocked in their hands, and each had four navy revolvers strapped upon him.

Brown, who appears to have separated from the others, was captured near Mill Springs late the same afternoon, May 21. After their flight from home the gang had formed a plan to make their way to Mexico.

Meyers and Brown, the survivors, were taken to New Madrid and safely lodged in jail, notwithstanding the high feeling against them. While there a young acquaintance of theirs named Mitchell was arrested. He was sixty miles away from all the shooting, but on hearing that his friends were in a scrape he started out to find them and give them a lift. He had no sooner began to make inquiries concerning them than he was seized and thrown into jail as an accomplice. Public excitement ran so high that the sheriff one night stealthily removed the prisoners and brought them to St. Louis for safe keeping. A special grand jury was called to indict them, and on the 14th of June, only a month after their first murder, and three weeks after they were arrested the trial was over. The jury was out twelve minutes. Judge J. D. Foster immediately sentenced Meyers and Brown to hang July 15. The odore Mitchell, for being a friend to the outlaw gang, was allowed to plead guilty to a charge of murder in the second degree and the judge sentenced him to the penitentiary for thirty years, remarking that he was the meanest of the gang.

PHILADELPHIA, Sept. 13.—Dr. Agnew in an interview to-night said that he did not regard the President's case as by any means a hopeless one, and added that he thought the President would receive much benefit from the pleasant weather which may reasonably be expected at Long Branch during this month and the next. Dr. Agnew stated emphatically that the President never had an abscess on the lung. It was merely a circumscribed inflammatory trouble in the nature of bronchial pneumonia.

The Followers of Wesley.

LONDON, Sept. 13.—The Methodist Ecumenical Conference to-day expressed strong feeling against the Methodists sending their children to Romish schools. On the subject of "Skepticism," Mr. Todd, of Philadelphia, said that skeptical science was a great enemy of the church.

The conference strongly condemned the theatres and dancing, Messrs. Diffen and Buckley, Americans, speaking in support of these opinions. Mr. Peck advocated religious entertainments as a counter attraction. A motion condemning the opium trade was introduced, but was referred to the business committee at the suggestion of Mr. Peck, because it contained words censuring the British government. A motion recommending legislation against the sale of liquor on Sunday will be submitted.

Rev. Robert Matlock, a preacher reported to have been lynched by a mob in the Boston mountains, in Arkansas, some six months ago, it seems was not lynched, as he was recently seen near Corsicana, in this state. Matlock was the starter of a new religion, a sort of mixture of all creeds, and soon had a crazy following about him. In his fanaticism he denounced all who would not think as he did, and was particularly severe on a family named Miller. Finally one of the family, a young man about 20 years old, told him he must stop his abuse of his family or take the consequences. Thus ill feelings arose between them, which culminated in their meeting one day at a public gathering where they talked the matter over and agreed to forgive and forget their differences and shook hands on it. As young Miller turned away, after they had taken awhile, Matlock suddenly drew a long knife and cut Miller's throat, severing his head nearly from his body. The excitement was tremendous, and an indignant crowd went in pursuit of the fleeing Matlock, and, as he was not seen afterwards, it was concluded he was caught and hung.

SERIOUS AFFRAY ON THE ISLAND. Desperate Encounter Between a Mob of Roughs and Two Police Officers.
One of the usual Sunday afternoon brawls on the Island happened yesterday afternoon. Ellen Duckett, a notorious colored "vag" and smasher generally, was drunk and creating a disturbance on Third and L streets southwest, and Officers Branson and Howell, of the First Precinct Station, attempted to arrest her. Immediately an immense mob led by her brother, Sam Duckett, a notorious thief and rowdy, surrounded the officers and tried to rescue the prisoner. A terrible fight ensued, in which Bransom was struck several times with stones and thrown down and his clothes nearly torn from his body, his club, badge, and belt, being wrenched away. Meanwhile Howell was wrestling with the Duckett woman, and, as she is as strong as any man, he had a hard time of it. During the scrimmage she bit his first finger nearly off, bit through the palm of his right hand, and laid his head open with a stone. Branson managed to release himself, and, drawing his pistol, fired, and saw a man drop to the ground face downwards. Branson rushed forward to secure his man, but was called by Howell to come to his rescue, and help take Ellen to the station-house, which they at last succeeded in doing. Returning to the scene of action they found that the man hit was Sam Duckett, and made vigilant search to find him, but he had been spirited away and it was impossible to discover his whereabouts. The officers continued searching until a late hour, but have not succeeded in finding him, he evidently having been secreted in some low shanty. From the way Duckett fell, the color of the blood, and the size of the pool it is presumed he was hit in the right side, near the region of the heart. Whether the wound is mortal remains to be seen. This Duckett woman has just returned from serving a six months' sentence in jail for biting Officer Branson's shoulder. Twelve of the participants in the fray have already been arrested and lodged in the station-house.

A very enjoyable Christmas entertainment occurred on Saturday evening at the New York Avenue Church. Practical charity was blended with the pleasure which the scholars of the Sunday school enjoyed, and in the room up-stairs contributions of groceries, money, clothing, &c., were liberally made for the poor of the Bethany and Gurley Missions. The children collected in the room down-stairs, and in one corner a series of beautiful tableaux held their attention and elicited numerous expressions of delight from the little ones. One tableau was entitled "The Choice," and another represented in a very effective way "The Closing and the Coming Year." These were interspersed with exercises appropriate to the occasion, under the direction of the superintendent, Mr. Williams. Two Policemen Attacked by a Mob. ONE OF THE OFFICERS SHOOTS A MAN.
The denizens of a neighborhood in South Washington called "Fredericksburg" made a serious assault on Policemen Branson and Howell, of the South Washington precinct, about 3 o'clock Sunday afternoon. Officer Howell attempted to arrest a notorious colored woman named Ellen Duckett, at the corner of 3d and M streets southwest, for being disorderly and blowing a tin horn on the street. She fought like a wildcat, and bit the officer's arms and hands. Within a few minutes there were at least fifteen hundred people on the spot, most of them colored. A large crowd of colored men and women attacked the officers with sticks and stones, and the fight lasted half an hour. Sam Duckett, Ellen's brother, who is a desperate character, was one of the foremost of the crowd of roughs that assaulted the officers. He had a large stone in his hand, with which he struck Officer Branson in the breast, and was in the act of picking up another stone when the policeman fired and Duckett fell. The officer, thinking he had killed his assailant, went to the assistance of his partner, who was hard pressed by the crowd and bleeding from bad cuts on the head and bites on the hands and arms. The woman was finally gotten to the station house and locked up. After relieving his partner Branson went to look for the man he had shot, but could find nothing but a pool of blood. The officers have received information that the bullet struck Duckett on the back of the head and glanced around between the scalp and the skull and came out at his forehead. In the Police Court yesterday Ellen Duckett was charged with assaulting Officer Howell. There being some doubt as to whether this court can send a prisoner to jail for a year, the court sentenced her to eleven months and twenty-nine days in jail. Sam Berry, one of the crowd, was charged with disorderly conduct, and fined $10 or 30 days in the workhouse. Agnes Ware, alias Lucas, was also arrested for being disorderly in the crowd, and was fined $5 or 15 days.

Christmas Boat Racing on the Potomac.

The Potomac Boat Club yesterday afternoon gave two races on the river. The first race, for single sculls, was called at one o'clock. The course was from the "Three Sisters," a mile down the river. W. F. Roberts, W. C. Bailey and A. W. Harrison, were the starters. Roberts took the lead. When the bridge was reached all three were well together. Harrison spurted and took the lead. Roberts tried to capture it from him but could not. Harrison came in first, Roberts second, and Bailey last. Time, 6 minutes, 30 seconds.

The second race was for four-oared shells. It was from opposite the Potomac boat-house to the Aqueduct and return. The light-weight crew consisted of Harrison, bow; Roberts, 2; Whittington, 3, and Barbarin stroke; colors, white. The heavy crew was Bailey, bow; Johnson, 2; Zappone, 3, and Doyle stroke; colors, red. There was a good race to the turn. The light-weightts started back with a lead of two lengths. The race was hotly contested. The light-weightts, however, went ahead with a spurt and crossed the line about a length ahead of the heavies. The time was 7 minutes and 4 seconds.

GUITEAU TRIAL CONTINUED.
DR. GRAY CROSS-EXAMINED.
HE THINKS THE PRISONER FEIGNING.
The witness having referred to the change in views among scientific men regarding insanity, the prisoner said: "Which shows that these experts don't know anything about it. They will swear to things to-day that they wouldn't have thought of swearing to 20 years ago and wouldn't swear to 20 years hence. The science of insanity is a progressive one."

Later the prisoner announced: "The idea that a man can't be insane without disease of the brain is nonsense. Read what the Saviour says. It is spiritology, not craniology, we want in this case."

The witness having said he was influenced in coming here by the advice of the president of the board of managers of the asylum, as well as the summons of the government, the prisoner asked: "How about Corkhill's money?"

Turning to the district attorney, the prisoner said: "He's got a bung hole up there at the Treasury which he had better shut off. He has run out $100,000 on this case I understand. He'll get shut off himself, I guess, before he's many days older. If I was President, he wouldn't be here a week. I will attend to him in '84 if Arthur doesn't attend to it before."

RECESS.

The court then, at 12:30, took a recess for half an hour.

GUITEAU ON THE AUTOGRAPH BUSINESS.

When the court reassembled Guiteau was the first to break silence. He said: "As there is nothing else to do, I might as will write my autographs for any one who wants them without money and without price. I wouldn't take—if I could get $500 for my autograph I wouldn't touch it. There's no money in this business for me. I don't care that there should be; I don't want any money about it—not one cent."

THE CROSS-EXAMINATION OF DR. GRAY

was then resumed by Mr. Scoville.

The witness said he had never had a case of insanity that he didn't find some disease of the body reflected in the brain, or some actual disease of the brain itself.

Mr. Scoville having asked if he had examined the brains of all his patients, the witness said:—
“We don't kill a man in order to examine his brain.”
“I didn't know what modern science might do,” remarked Mr. Scoville.

GUITEAU ON KILLING A MAN TO EXAMINE HIS BRAIN.

“That's the way these fellows do,” said the prisoner. “They kill a man and then examine his brain. That's what the experts are trying to do on this case, I suppose.”

Mr. Scoville questioned the witness upon an article he published in 1874 in the American Journal of Insanity on the “Pathology of Insanity.”
“Write something, doctor, on spiritology of insanity, next time,” interjected the prisoner.

FEIGNED INSANITY.

The witness said he had investigated 40 or 50 cases of feigned insanity.

“Did you ever,” asked Mr. Scoville, “know of any case of feigned insanity like that of the prisoner?”

“I have not considered,” the witness replied, “that the prisoner at the bar has made any manifestation of insanity.”

The witness was asked if he had not testified that the prisoner was feigning, and he replied that he said he was feigning in so far as he tried to impress people that he was acting under an inspiration.

Mr. Scoville asked to have evidence on this point stricken out, as “now he has”—began Mr. Scoville, “Put his toot into it,” interjected the prisoner.

“Let the cat out of the bag,” continued Mr. Scoville.

The witness has now declared that his belief is “that the prisoner is telling a lie.”

The witness insisted that he based his judgment on the prisoner's conduct.

“It is a fact for the jury to pass upon,” said the prisoner, “whether he refers to the testimony or my conduct.”

The witness said he did not pass upon the question whether the prisoner was lying or not.

“I never lie, sir,” shouted the prisoner.

The court overruled Mr. Scoville's objection to the testimony.

“All your talk is different from what you said yesterday,” said the prisoner to the witness. “Corkhill must have demoralized you last night.”
"All your talk is different from what you said yesterday," said the prisoner to the witness. "Corkhill must have demoralized you last night? How much are you going to get for this extra work? It ought to be worth about a thousand dollars more than it was yesterday."

The witness, having declined to answer a question categorically, the prisoner remarked: "The doctor is getting badly demoralized this afternoon."

Mr. Scoville having questioned the witness in reference to the delusions of drunken men, the prisoner said: "According to your philosophy, doctor, a man can't get drunk or crazy without his brain is diseased. That shows how much you know about it."

The witness said insanity could not be produced by fear or other emotions without an intermediate physical disturbance. This disturbance might come from the quickened action of the heart, cau sing a fusion of blood in the brain.

GUITEAU'S NEW YEAR GREETING.

The cross-examination dragged along until nearly 3 o'clock, when the prisoner stopped it by saying: "It's most 3 o'clock, Scoville. To-morrow will be New Year's day, 1882. I receive my calls this year at the jail; any one who comes can get in. I will be glad to see any one who comes. I wish everybody a happy New Year's."

The court was then adjourned till Tuesday.

ABERDEEN, Miss., December 13.—The murderer of the Walker brothers is still at large. The negro under arrest has, after severe torture, told the story of the horrible scene. The negro was passing along the highway, and was attracted by a camp fire some distance from the road. One man was there awake by the fire, while the other three boys were asleep on a bed spread out before it. This man beckoned to the negro to come there, and disclosed to him his deadly purpose, saying to the negro that there was money in it, and promised to give him $200 for his aid in the execution of the blackest of deeds. The negro describes the procedure—the younger brother was asleep in the middle. The first killed was the youngest, who received two blows on the head with the ax; the next in age was the second victim. By this time the oldest brother had opened his eyes and raised his head, when the monster struck him one blow on the head that killed him instantly. They then covered the bodies with blankets, and after rifling their pockets of a watch and sixty dollars, the man handed the negro the ax, telling him to throw it out of sight, then mounted a mule, and has not been seen since.

The defense set up insanity. The jury was out an hour and a half. The verdict gives great satisfaction, as the public are getting rather tired of the insanity plea in murder cases. Vescamp was sentenced to the State's prison for life, the extreme penalty in this State.

Wife-Murder and Suicide.

DETROIT, December 13.—A double tragedy occurred at Cold Water at an early hour this morning in a house of ill-fame kept by Mrs. Nettie Wheeler, better known as "Net Davis." While entertaining some company about 1 o'clock with vulgar songs, sung by herself and her girls, her husband called her into the kitchen and remonstrated against any further singing of the sort, when she replied, "I will not, if you wish it." He immediately shot her through the breast, when she ran to the parlor and fell dead. The murderer then put three bullets into his own body, which resulted fatally at once. Jealousy was the supposed cause.

Tired of Life.

CINCINNATI, December 13.—The Gazette's Dayton (O.) special says that Mason S. Hamilton shot himself to-day in the oathhouse of a saloon, and when found was insensible. The ball having entered his head near the left eye and passed out near the ear, the surgeon declared that death was inevitable. He left a letter to the Coroner, saying that he took his own life because of ill health and inability longer to enjoy life. He was Captain of Company H of the Eleventh Indiana Cavalry during the war; had been County Surveyor of Butler county and City Solicitor of Hamilton, Ohio. For the past two years he had been an inmate of the Soldiers' Home.

DETROIT, December 13.—J. W. Dixon, the man arrested on the charge of having murdered Wm. J. Phillips, the drover, in Sanitac county, as telegraphed yesterday, died this morning in jail from the effects of laudanum taken early Monday morning. He was informed by his physician that he could not possibly live, and was asked if he had anything to say. He replied: "No; nothing. I want to die." He was delirious most of last night, but would divulge nothing, and would often repeat the words, "Poor Phillips! he is dead!" The prosecution had worked up a strong case against Dixon. Phillips was known to have been on the up train November 25th, and got off at Amadore. That same day Dixon hired a rig at Lexington, which he returned the following day. The night of the 25th he called at a farmhouse, near Amadore, and asked for a pair of hot water, saying his horse was foundered. The folks noticed blood on his hands, and a boy says he saw him washing the buggy. The buggy was examined yesterday, and clots of blood found in the crevices. Dixon had also displayed large amounts of money within the last two weeks, which was something very unusual with him. He also tried to purchase a brick block at Lexington, offering $3000 cash for it. Telegrams had passed between Phillips and Dixon, which the prosecution were unable to get at present, but it is thought they will be conclusive of his guilt. Dixon's relatives live at Mount Clemens, and he leaves a family. Some years since he was sent to the State prison for forgery.

AT THE SCENE OF HIS CRIME.

Detective Bean Arrives at Aberdeen With Bob Jones, the Murderer of the Walker Brothers.

The Villain Makes a Full Confession of the Terrible Crime, in All its Hideous Details.

Special to the Appeal.]

ABERDEEN, Miss., December 24.—Mr. Rush O. Bean, the detective who left here some days ago in search of Bob Jones, the murderer of the three Walker boys killed near here about one month ago, arrived in Aberdeen last night with the prisoner. For the capture of this villain Mr. Bean deserves not only the rewards he received, but the thanks of all interested in peace and the sanctity of society. The miserable wretch evaded, lied and dissembled to such an extent that eavesdropping was found necessary, and this being done the listener succeeded in hearing the plot of the murder, the deed and all subsequent transactions, as William Miller, the negro accomplice, was incarcerated with Jones in the same cage; however, to make sure of the identity and guilt, to-night the negro was taken from jail under the threat and pretext of being lynched. This left Jones alone in his dreary dungeon, in darkness and horror. Two gentlemen then approached Jones, and, after diligent effort, succeeded in procuring a full confession to the heinous crime. He confessed having split the heads of the three boys as they lay by the fireside of their camp beside the road, having taken their money, and his escape and subsequent flight and capture. This murder being the most horrible ever known in this community, great interest was felt, and his capture is a relief to this entire section. He will be tried with Miller at a special term of the court, and they will speedily be sent to the happy hunting grounds.

The Aberdeen Murder.
A NEGRO ACCOMPLICE TELLS HOW THE DEED WAS DONE.
The murderer of the Walker brothers is still at large. The negro under arrest has, after close questioning, told the story of the horrible scene. The negro was passing along the highway, and was attracted by a camp fire some distance from the road. One man was there awake by the fire, while the other three boys were asleep on a bed spread out before it. This man beckoned to the negro to come there, and disclosed to him his deadly purpose, saying to the negro that there was money in it, and promised to give him $200 for his aid in the execution of the blackest of deeds. The negro describes the procedure—the younger brother was asleep in the middle. The first killed was the youngest, who received two blows on the head with the ax; the next in age was the second victim. By this time the oldest brother had opened his eyes and raised his head, when the monster struck him one blow on the head that killed him instantly. They then covered the bodies with blankets, and after rifling their pockets of a watch and sixty dollars, the man handed the negro the ax, telling him to throw it out of sight, then mounted a mule, and has not been seen since.
